title: Overview and justification
body:
This course is about working with how university learning, assessment and feedback are set up, so you can act on them in your own study. By the end you will be able to work out how a module is designed, interpret marking criteria, and use the feedback cycle to turn comments into improvements.

You already know what learning, assessment and feedback are. This course takes the next step: it shows you how they are built, and how to use that knowledge to get more from your course and better marks for your work.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: work out how a module's learning is designed so you can engage with it on its own terms
interpret marking criteria to see what your work needs to show
use the feedback cycle to turn feedback into improvements in your work.

title: In real academic practice
body: Working with the system is what separates a student who drifts through modules from one who gets the most out of them. Knowing why a seminar is built as it is, what a marking grid rewards, and how to act on feedback are habits you use in every module, in every subject. Build them now and each assignment becomes easier to target.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, how your learning is designed: why sessions are built the way they are, and what that asks of you. Second, reading marking criteria: how to see what a marker is looking for. Third, making feedback work: the cycle that turns comments into better work. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, tasks and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, mark or comment you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can work out how a module's learning is designed and engage with it on its own terms.
I can interpret marking criteria to see what my work needs to show.
I can use the feedback cycle to turn feedback into improvements in my work.

title: Orientation
body: You already know that you are expected to be active at university rather than to sit and absorb. This lesson looks at the reasons behind that expectation: how tutors design the sessions you attend, and why they build them the way they do. Once you can see the design, you can work with it instead of guessing what is wanted.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are past simply noticing that university learning is different from school. The aim now is to read the design of a session or module and act on it, so that you prepare for a seminar or a lecture in the way its design intends.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: distinguish active, constructivist learning from passive, behaviourist learning in how a session is designed
explain why tutors design a session backwards from its intended learning outcomes
work out how to engage with a learning activity in {{context}} on its own terms.

title: Concept: definition
body:
University learning is designed on the premise that you will engage with it actively. Most of it rests on constructivism, the idea that you build understanding by doing: discussing, applying and working things out, rather than being told. A smaller part rests on behaviourism, where a clear, step-by-step process trains you to do something, such as a library search. Each has its place.

Tutors also design backwards. They begin with the intended learning outcomes, the things you should be able to do by the end, and then build the activities and content to lead there. This is called constructive alignment. When you can see the outcomes a session is aimed at, you can see what its activities are for.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: How a session is designed, backwards
body: A session is planned from its end point. Reveal each stage to see how a tutor works back from the outcomes to the room.
instruction: Select each stage to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Start with the outcomes
_items.body: The tutor begins at the end. They write the intended learning outcomes: what you should be able to do by the close, usually as a verb such as analyse or apply.

_items.title: Choose the activities
_items.body: Working backwards, the tutor picks activities that make you practise those outcomes. If the outcome is to analyse, you are asked to analyse something, not just to hear about analysis.

_items.title: Select the content
_items.body: Only now is the content chosen, and only what the activities need. Readings and explanations are there to feed the activity, not to be covered for their own sake.

_items.title: Alignment in the room
_items.body: By the session itself, outcomes, activities and content all point the same way. This is constructive alignment. Spot the outcome and you can see what every part of the session is for.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students see the same tutorial on their timetable, with a pre-task: read one article and come ready to argue whether its claim holds.

{{learner-a}} reads the article and highlights the main points to revise later. In the tutorial, {{learner-a}} waits to be told what the article means. The session is built around a debate, but {{learner-a}} has prepared as if it were a lecture, so there is little to contribute. This treats an active design as a passive one.

{{learner-b}} notices the pre-task is asking for a judgement, so prepares one: the claim, what it rests on, and a reason it might be challenged. In the tutorial, {{learner-b}} joins the debate straight away. By reading the design of the session, {{learner-b}} arrived able to do the very thing it was built for.

Both students did the reading. Only {{learner-b}} worked out what the session was designed to make them do, and prepared for that.

title: Reading the design of a session
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These habits turn a timetable into something you can work with. Try them on your next session.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I found the intended learning outcomes for this module or session?
Have I worked out what each activity is asking me to practise?
Have I spotted whether a session is built around doing (constructivist) or a set process (behaviourist)?
Have I prepared in the way the activity needs, not just by reading?
Have I asked what the content is for, rather than trying to cover all of it?
Have I checked how this session links to the assessment it is preparing me for?

title: Formative check: active versus passive design
displayTitle: A tutorial is built around a group debate rather than a tutor explanation. Which kind of learning design is this, and what does it ask of you?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A tutorial built around a debate is which kind of design?

_items.text: Constructivist design: it asks you to build understanding by taking part.
_items.feedback: Yes. A debate is learning by doing; it expects you to participate, not absorb.

_items.text: Behaviourist design: it asks you to follow a fixed process.
_items.feedback: Behaviourist design trains a set process; a debate is open and participatory.

_items.text: It is not really a design; the tutor simply ran out of slides.
_items.feedback: A debate is a deliberate design choice, not an absence of planning.

_items.text: Passive design: it asks you to take notes and absorb.
_items.feedback: A debate is the opposite of passive; it needs your active contribution.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A debate is constructivist design: it expects you to build understanding by taking part.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a debate asks you to DO, compared with a lecture.
_incorrect.final: A debate is constructivist design: it is learning by doing and expects you to participate, not to sit and absorb.

title: Formative check: constructive alignment
displayTitle: Why does a tutor decide the intended learning outcomes before planning the activities and content?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why are outcomes decided before activities and content?

_items.text: So the activities and content can be built to lead you to those outcomes.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is constructive alignment: everything is designed backwards from the outcomes.

_items.text: Because the outcomes are the hardest part and are best done first.
_items.feedback: It is not about difficulty; the outcomes set the direction everything else follows.

_items.text: Because the content must be chosen before anyone knows what it is for.
_items.feedback: It is the reverse: the purpose (the outcomes) is set first, then the content to serve it.

_items.text: So the session can cover as much material as possible.
_items.feedback: Alignment is about purpose, not coverage; content is chosen to serve the outcomes.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Deciding outcomes first lets the tutor align activities and content to them, which is constructive alignment.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about the activities and content leading you to the outcomes.
_incorrect.final: Outcomes are set first so the activities and content can be aligned to lead you to them. This backward design is constructive alignment.

title: Formative check: engaging on its own terms
displayTitle: A session in {{context}} lists an outcome: 'by the end you will be able to apply the method to a new case'. How should you engage with it on its own terms?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How should you engage with a session whose outcome is to apply a method?

_items.text: Come ready to apply the method yourself, not just to watch it explained.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, an 'apply' outcome means the session is built for you to practise applying it.

_items.text: Memorise the definition of the method for a later test.
_items.feedback: Memorising a definition is not applying; the outcome asks you to use the method.

_items.text: Wait for the tutor to work through every case for you.
_items.feedback: That treats an active design as passive; the outcome expects you to apply it yourself.

_items.text: Read widely around the topic and hope the outcome sorts itself out.
_items.feedback: Background reading is not the same as practising the applied move the outcome names.

_feedback.correct: That's right. An 'apply' outcome in {{context}} means the session is designed for you to practise applying the method yourself.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The outcome uses the verb 'apply'; what does that ask you to come ready to do?
_incorrect.final: An 'apply' outcome means engaging by practising the method yourself in {{context}}, not by memorising, watching or only reading around it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a recent seminar or workshop in your subject. What was it designed to make you do, and did you prepare for that, or did you prepare as though it were a lecture?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: University learning is designed to be active. Most of it is constructivist, building understanding through doing, with some behaviourist, process-driven training alongside. Tutors design backwards from intended learning outcomes, so every activity and reading has a purpose you can see. You can now tell active design from passive, explain constructive alignment, and work out how to engage with a session on its own terms. The next lesson turns to how your work is then judged.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 36 to 39 of Chapter 3, 'Defining learning at university', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: When your work comes back with a mark, the mark was not a guess. It was reached against a set of marking criteria: a grid of levels and descriptors your tutor used to judge the work. This lesson shows you how to read that grid, so you can see what a marker is looking for before you hand anything in.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have met marks and grades already. The step here is to stop treating the criteria as background and start using them: reading the descriptors, working out where a piece of work sits, and letting that shape what you produce. Applying criteria to grade others' work, or your own, comes later.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: interpret the levels and descriptors in a set of marking criteria
work out how a tutor reaches an overall mark across several criteria
use marking criteria to decide what a piece of work in {{context}} needs to show.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Marking criteria are the measures a tutor uses to decide what mark your work should get. A criterion, such as knowledge and understanding, is split into levels, each with a band of marks and a descriptor that names the quality of work at that level. Knowledge might move from 'limited' to 'basic', 'some', 'detailed' and 'developed' as the marks rise.

To mark your work, a tutor decides which level it sits at on each criterion, then weighs those together into an overall mark. A piece might be strong on knowledge but only clear on communication, which pulls the final figure between the two. Reading the descriptors tells you, in advance, what the top band actually asks for.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What a marking grid rewards
body: A grid usually marks several criteria at once. Review each card to see what the top band asks for.
instruction: Read through the cards below.

_items.title: Knowledge and understanding
_items.subtitle: What you know
_items.text: Low bands show 'basic' or 'limited' understanding. The top band shows 'developed' understanding: accurate, in depth, and used to make a point, not just stated.

_items.title: Communication
_items.subtitle: How you say it
_items.text: Low bands are unclear or merely basic. The top band is clear and precise, with structure that guides the reader. How you write is marked, not only what you write.

_items.title: Critical evaluation
_items.subtitle: What you do with sources
_items.text: Low bands show 'basic' engagement with sources. The top band shows 'developed' engagement: you weigh and use the literature, rather than listing it.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are given the same essay brief and the marking grid that will be used on it.

{{learner-a}} skims the brief, writes everything known about the topic, and hands it in. The grid was there all along, but {{learner-a}} never read it. The work is full of knowledge, yet it lists sources without weighing them, so critical evaluation stays in the lower band and the mark disappoints.

{{learner-b}} reads the grid first and notices that the top band for critical evaluation asks you to weigh sources, not list them. So {{learner-b}} plans the essay around that: each source is used and judged, not just cited. The knowledge is similar to {{learner-a}}'s, but the work now reaches a higher band where it counts.

Both students knew the topic. Only {{learner-b}} read the criteria and built the work to meet them.

title: Using the marking grid
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These habits turn a marking grid into a plan for your work. Try them on your next assignment.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I found the marking criteria for this assignment, in the handbook or on the VLE?
Have I read the top-band descriptor for each criterion, not just the mark I want?
Have I worked out which word changes between bands, such as 'basic' to 'developed'?
Have I checked which criteria carry the most weight in this task?
Have I planned my work to show what the top band actually asks for?
Have I used the criteria to review a draft before I submit?

title: Formative check: interpreting descriptors
displayTitle: A grid describes the top band for 'knowledge and understanding' as 'developed' and the band below as 'detailed'. What does moving from 'detailed' to 'developed' ask of your work?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does moving from 'detailed' to 'developed' knowledge ask for?

_items.text: Deeper, more fully worked understanding, used to make a point.
_items.feedback: Yes. Higher bands reward depth and use of understanding, not just more facts.

_items.text: A greater number of sources cited.
_items.feedback: Citation count sits under critical evaluation, not the knowledge descriptor.

_items.text: Longer paragraphs with the same content.
_items.feedback: Length is not quality; the band is about depth of understanding.

_items.text: The same understanding, written more quickly.
_items.feedback: Speed is irrelevant; the descriptor is about how developed the understanding is.

_feedback.correct: That's right. 'Developed' asks for deeper, more fully worked understanding than 'detailed', not simply more material.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The descriptors describe the quality of understanding; what does 'developed' add over 'detailed'?
_incorrect.final: Moving to 'developed' asks for deeper, more fully worked understanding. More sources, more length or more speed do not raise this band.

title: Formative check: reaching an overall mark
displayTitle: A piece of work is 'developed' on knowledge, only 'clear' on communication, and shows 'some' critical evaluation. How does a tutor reach the overall mark?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How is an overall mark reached across several criteria?

_items.text: They judge each criterion's level, then weigh them together into one mark that reflects the mix.
_items.feedback: Yes. The mark reflects the balance across criteria, not any single band.

_items.text: They simply take the top band, since knowledge is strongest.
_items.feedback: The strongest criterion does not set the whole mark; the others pull it down.

_items.text: They add the three percentages and divide by three for an exact average.
_items.feedback: Marking is a judgement across criteria, not a strict arithmetic average.

_items.text: They use communication alone, as it is easiest to see.
_items.feedback: No single criterion decides the mark; all are weighed together.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The tutor judges each criterion's level and weighs them together, so the mark reflects the overall mix.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. One criterion does not decide the mark; think about how they are combined.
_incorrect.final: The tutor judges each criterion's level, then weighs them together into one mark reflecting the mix, rather than taking the top band or a strict average.

title: Formative check: using the criteria
displayTitle: You are about to write a piece in {{context}} and the top band of the grid rewards 'developed engagement with academic sources'. What should the work show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should the work show to meet 'developed engagement with sources'?

_items.text: Sources that are weighed and used to build your point, not just listed.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, developed engagement means judging and using sources, not listing them.

_items.text: As many references as you can fit in.
_items.feedback: Quantity is not engagement; the band rewards how you weigh and use sources.

_items.text: One trusted source, quoted at length.
_items.feedback: Leaning on a single quotation is not developed engagement with the literature.

_items.text: Your own opinion, with sources left out to keep it original.
_items.feedback: Dropping sources removes the engagement the criterion rewards.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, 'developed engagement' means weighing and using sources to build your point.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. The descriptor is about how you handle sources; which option weighs and uses them?
_incorrect.final: Developed engagement in {{context}} means sources that are weighed and used to build your point, not merely listed, piled up or dropped.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Find the marking criteria for an assignment you have coming up. Which criterion do you think your work is currently weakest on, and what does the top-band descriptor ask for there?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Marking criteria are a grid of levels and descriptors a tutor uses to judge your work and reach a mark. Reading the descriptors, especially the top band, tells you what each criterion rewards, and seeing how the levels are weighed together explains how an overall mark is reached. You can now interpret criteria, work out how a mark is built, and use the grid to decide what a piece of work needs to show. The next lesson turns to the feedback that comes back with the mark.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 67 to 73 of Chapter 5, 'Understanding Assessment', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: Feedback is easy to skim, feel briefly about, and forget. Yet the comments that come back with a mark are the clearest guide you will get to improving the next piece. This lesson gives you a way to work through feedback so it changes what you do, rather than just how you feel.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You have received feedback before. The step here is to stop reading it as a verdict on work that is finished, and start using it as instructions for work to come. That means a repeatable process you can run on any feedback, in any module.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: order the four stages of the feedback cycle and say what each one does
turn a feedback comment into a concrete action
choose the feedback-cycle move that fits a situation in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Feedback is best treated as diagnostic: it tells you where your work is strong and where it needs to grow, so it points forward to the next piece, not back at the one just marked. Getting value from it is a skill, and it depends on your mindset. A fixed-mindset reader skims the comments; a growth-mindset reader uses them to drive improvement.

The feedback cycle gives you four stages to work through. Review: read the feedback and form an overall impression. Interpret: study each comment against the marking criteria and your own work. Articulate: turn what you find into an action plan. Apply: carry those actions into your next piece of work. The hard, valuable stage is turning comments into actions.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The four stages of the feedback cycle
body: The feedback cycle has four stages, worked in order. Reveal each one to see what it asks of you.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: 1. Review
_items.body: Read the feedback through and take it in. Is it reasonable? Does any of it surprise you? Is anything missing? This stage is about forming an overall impression, not fixing anything yet.

_items.title: 2. Interpret
_items.body: Look closely at each comment and read it against the marking criteria and your own work. Split it into what went well and what did not, and find where in your work each comment points. This is where the real understanding happens.

_items.title: 3. Articulate
_items.body: Turn your interpretation into an action plan: specific, doable steps for next time. 'Be more critical' becomes 'weigh each source instead of describing it'. This is the stage students most often skip, and the one that carries the value.

_items.title: 4. Apply
_items.body: Carry those actions into your next piece of work. Feedback only improves anything when it changes what you actually do. The cycle then begins again on the new work.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students get the same comment back on an essay: 'well researched, but you describe your sources rather than weighing them'.

{{learner-a}} reads the comment, feels the sting of the 'but', and files the essay away. Nothing is wrong with the reading, but it stops at feeling. Next time, the same comment comes back, because {{learner-a}} never turned it into anything to do differently.

{{learner-b}} runs the cycle. Review: the comment seems fair. Interpret: it maps to the critical-evaluation criterion, and the sources really were just summarised. Articulate: the action is 'after each source, add a sentence judging how strong it is'. Apply: the next essay does exactly that, and the criterion improves.

Both read the same comment. Only {{learner-b}} carried it through to an action and a better next piece.

title: Running the feedback cycle
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These habits turn a comment into a better next piece. Try them on your next returned assignment.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I read all the feedback through once before reacting to any single comment?
Have I matched each comment to the marking criteria it refers to?
Have I found where in my work each comment points?
Have I turned each useful comment into a specific, doable action?
Have I written the actions somewhere I will see them for the next piece?
Have I applied at least one action to my next assignment?

title: Formative check: ordering the cycle
displayTitle: What is the right order of the four stages of the feedback cycle?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the correct order of the feedback cycle?

_items.text: Review, Interpret, Articulate, Apply.
_items.feedback: Yes. You take it in, make sense of it, plan actions, then carry them out.

_items.text: Apply, Review, Interpret, Articulate.
_items.feedback: You cannot apply actions before you have worked out what they are.

_items.text: Interpret, Review, Apply, Articulate.
_items.feedback: You review the feedback before you interpret it, and articulate actions before applying them.

_items.text: Articulate, Apply, Review, Interpret.
_items.feedback: Articulating actions comes after reviewing and interpreting, not first.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Review, Interpret, Articulate, Apply: take it in, make sense of it, plan, then act.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the natural order: you cannot plan or act before you have read and understood the feedback.
_incorrect.final: The order is Review, Interpret, Articulate, Apply. You read the feedback, make sense of it, turn it into actions, then carry them out.

title: Formative check: turning a comment into an action
displayTitle: A tutor writes: 'your argument is hard to follow in places'. Which response is turning the comment into a concrete action, the Articulate stage?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response is the Articulate stage: turning the comment into an action?

_items.text: Plan to add a signpost sentence at the start of each paragraph in the next essay.
_items.feedback: Yes. That is a specific, doable step for next time: the Articulate stage.

_items.text: Decide that the tutor simply did not read carefully.
_items.feedback: That dismisses the comment rather than turning it into an action.

_items.text: Feel disappointed and move on to the next module.
_items.feedback: Feeling is not action; the comment never changes what you do.

_items.text: Reread the comment several times without changing anything.
_items.feedback: Rereading is part of Review; it is not yet a concrete action.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Planning a specific step, such as signposting each paragraph, is the Articulate stage in action.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Articulate means a specific, doable step; which option names one?
_incorrect.final: Turning the comment into an action means a concrete step such as signposting each paragraph. Dismissing, feeling or rereading do not change what you do.

title: Formative check: choosing the move
displayTitle: You get feedback on a piece in {{context}} and you are not sure which comments matter most. Which feedback-cycle move helps here?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which feedback-cycle move helps when you are unsure which comments matter most?

_items.text: Interpret: read each comment against the marking criteria to see what it points to.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, interpreting against the criteria shows which comments carry weight.

_items.text: Apply: start rewriting before you have understood the comments.
_items.feedback: Applying before understanding risks acting on the wrong things.

_items.text: Skip to a new topic to avoid the difficult parts.
_items.feedback: Avoiding the feedback means it never improves your work.

_items.text: Articulate an action plan before reading the comments.
_items.feedback: You cannot plan actions before you have interpreted what the comments mean.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Interpreting each comment against the criteria in {{context}} shows which ones matter most.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which stage is about making sense of the comments against the criteria?
_incorrect.final: When you are unsure which comments matter, the Interpret stage helps: read each against the marking criteria in {{context}} to see what it points to.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last piece of feedback you received. Did you turn any of it into something to do differently, or did it stop at how it made you feel? What is one action you could still take from it?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and there are no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Feedback is diagnostic: it points forward to your next piece of work. The feedback cycle gives you four stages to make that happen: Review, Interpret, Articulate and Apply. The stage that carries the value, and the one most often skipped, is Articulate: turning a comment into a concrete action. You can now order the cycle, turn comments into actions, and choose the move a situation needs. With learning design, marking criteria and feedback in hand, you can work with the system rather than guess at it.

title: Lesson Sources
instruction: This lesson draws on the following source.

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.
A workshop is built around a hands-on task you complete in pairs, rather than a talk you listen to. What kind of learning design is this?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A workshop built around a hands-on task is which kind of design?

_items.text: Constructivist: you build understanding by doing.
_items.feedback: Yes. Learning by doing is constructivist design.

_items.text: Behaviourist: a fixed process trains a single skill.
_items.feedback: A hands-on, open task is not a fixed training process.

_items.text: Passive: it is designed for you to absorb.
_items.feedback: A hands-on task is active, not passive.

_items.text: Unplanned: there is no real design behind it.
_items.feedback: A paired task is a deliberate design choice.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Learning by doing is constructivist design.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a hands-on, paired task asks you to do.

body: Why do tutors decide a session's intended learning outcomes before choosing its activities and content?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why are outcomes decided before activities and content?

_items.text: So the activities and content can be aligned to lead you to those outcomes.
_items.feedback: Yes. That backward design is constructive alignment.

_items.text: Because outcomes are a formality added at the end.
_items.feedback: Outcomes are the starting point of the design, not a formality.

_items.text: So the session can cover the maximum amount of material.
_items.feedback: Alignment is about purpose, not coverage.

_items.text: Because content must always be chosen before its purpose is known.
_items.feedback: It is the reverse: purpose first, then content.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Outcomes are set first so activities and content can be aligned to them.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the outcomes are for in the design.

body: In a marking grid, what does a descriptor such as 'developed' or 'basic' tell you?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does a descriptor such as 'developed' or 'basic' tell you?

_items.text: The quality of work expected in that band for that criterion.
_items.feedback: Yes. Descriptors name the quality of work at each band.

_items.text: The number of sources you must cite.
_items.feedback: Descriptors describe quality, not a source count.

_items.text: The exact word count required.
_items.feedback: Descriptors are about quality, not length.

_items.text: How long the tutor will take to mark it.
_items.feedback: Descriptors describe your work, not the marking time.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A descriptor names the quality of work expected in that band.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Descriptors describe the quality of the work at each level.

body: Work is 'developed' on knowledge but only 'basic' on critical evaluation. How is the overall mark reached?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: How is an overall mark reached when criteria differ?

_items.text: The levels on each criterion are weighed together into one mark.
_items.feedback: Yes. The mark reflects the balance across criteria.

_items.text: The highest band always decides the whole mark.
_items.feedback: The strongest criterion does not set the whole mark.

_items.text: Only critical evaluation counts towards the mark.
_items.feedback: All criteria are weighed, not just one.

_items.text: The marks are averaged to an exact midpoint regardless of quality.
_items.feedback: Marking is a judgement across criteria, not a strict average.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The levels across criteria are weighed together into one mark.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. No single criterion decides the mark; how are they combined?

body: What is the correct order of the feedback cycle?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the correct order of the feedback cycle?

_items.text: Review, Interpret, Articulate, Apply.
_items.feedback: Yes. Take it in, make sense of it, plan, then act.

_items.text: Apply, Articulate, Interpret, Review.
_items.feedback: That reverses the cycle; you cannot apply before you understand.

_items.text: Interpret, Apply, Review, Articulate.
_items.feedback: Review comes first, and you articulate actions before applying them.

_items.text: Review, Apply, Interpret, Articulate.
_items.feedback: You interpret and articulate before you apply.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Review, Interpret, Articulate, Apply.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. You cannot act before you have read and understood the feedback.

body: A comment says 'you describe sources rather than weighing them'. Which is turning it into an action (Articulate)?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which response turns the comment into an action?

_items.text: Add a sentence judging each source's strength in the next essay.
_items.feedback: Yes. A specific, doable step is the Articulate stage.

_items.text: Decide the comment is unfair and ignore it.
_items.feedback: Dismissing a comment is not turning it into an action.

_items.text: Reread the comment until it feels less harsh.
_items.feedback: Rereading does not change what you do.

_items.text: Wait and hope the next tutor marks differently.
_items.feedback: Hoping is not an action you can take on your work.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A specific step, such as judging each source, is the Articulate stage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option names a concrete step for the next piece?

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. The way your course is built is no longer a mystery you have to guess at. You can work out how a module's learning is designed, and engage with a session in the way it intends. You can read a marking grid and see what each band rewards, so you know what your work needs to show. And you can run the feedback cycle, turning comments into actions that improve the next piece. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, working with the system is something you do in every module. Each time you read a brief against its criteria, prepare for a seminar in the way it is designed, or turn feedback into an action, you are using these habits. They pay off across your degree, and the same ability to read what is wanted and act on it is what professional work rewards too.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the advanced course in this pathway takes you into assessing your own and others' work and aligning your whole practice to the learning, assessment and feedback cycle. Going wider: the same habits support Academic Writing, Reflective Practice and Revising and Exams, where you put them to work on real tasks.

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: how your learning is designed, how your work is marked against criteria, and how to use feedback. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one connected cycle you can work with.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to run the whole cycle perfectly. The aim is to see design, marking and feedback as one connected system rather than three separate ideas, so that you can work with it in every module you take.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: connect how your learning is designed, how your work is marked, and how feedback is used as one cycle
analyse how the three work as one in a student's study across a module
apply the three together to your own study in {{context}}

title: Concept: definition
body: Working with the whole cycle means treating design, marking and feedback as one connected loop rather than three separate things. A module is designed backwards from its intended outcomes. The marking criteria put those same outcomes into words, so they tell you what your work must show. Feedback is judged against those criteria, and it points forward into your next piece of work. Read one part and it tells you about the others.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, working with the whole cycle means starting each module by reading how it is built and what its criteria reward, then using every piece of feedback to aim the next piece better. A quick look at the design, the criteria and the last feedback, treated as one picture, is worth more than handling each on its own. Over a module, those connected moves add up.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about a module you are taking now. How is it designed, what do its marking criteria reward, and what has your feedback told you so far? Pick one thing you could do differently to work with the whole cycle.
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

You read how a module is built, aim your work at what its criteria reward, and use feedback to improve the next piece. It is the connected habit, not any single part, that gets more from your studies.

title: The practice as one cycle
displayTitle: The practice as one cycle
body: Design, marking and feedback work as one connected loop, not three separate things. Select each part of the cycle to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each part of the cycle.

_items.title: Read the design
_items.body: Work out how the module is designed, and what its sessions are built to make you do.

_items.title: Check the criteria
_items.body: Read the marking criteria to see what your work needs to show, since they put the module's outcomes into words.

_items.title: Do the work
_items.body: Do the work and hand it in, aiming at what the criteria reward.

_items.title: Use the feedback
_items.body: Use the feedback, against those same criteria, to improve your next piece - which starts the cycle again.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students take the same module and get the same feedback on an early essay. One treats each part on its own: she reads the brief, writes, and skims the mark. The other reads how the module is designed, checks the criteria before writing, and uses the feedback to plan the next essay. Over the term the second student's work improves, because she worked with the whole cycle rather than three separate tasks.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to work with the whole cycle
body: Use these to work with the whole cycle on a module, rather than treating each part on its own.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I work out how this module is designed, and what its sessions ask of me?
Did I read the marking criteria before starting, not just after the mark?
Did I aim my work at what the criteria actually reward?
Did I read my feedback against those same criteria?
Did I carry one change forward into my next piece of work?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat design, marking and feedback as one connected cycle rather than three separate things?
body: Why is it more useful to treat design, marking and feedback as one connected cycle rather than three separate things?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat design, marking and feedback as one connected cycle rather than three separate things?

_items.text: Because each part points to the others: the design aims at outcomes, the criteria put those outcomes into words, and feedback shows you how to meet them next time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Read one part and it tells you about the others, so the whole module makes sense.

_items.text: Because once you see the design you can ignore the marking criteria.
_items.feedback: The criteria matter as much as the design. They tell you what your work must show.

_items.text: Because treating them as one means you never have to act on feedback.
_items.feedback: Feedback is part of the cycle. Working with the cycle means acting on it, not skipping it.

_items.text: Because one connected cycle takes less effort than learning three things.
_items.feedback: It is not about less effort. Seeing the links makes each part easier to act on.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The three parts are aimed at the same outcomes, so each one tells you about the others.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the three parts share, and how each one helps you read the next.

displayTitle: A student reads how a module is designed, checks the marking criteria before writing, and uses the feedback on each essay to plan the next. Over the term her work improves. What does this show?
body: A student reads how a module is designed, checks the marking criteria before writing, and uses the feedback on each essay to plan the next. Over the term her work improves. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reads how a module is designed, checks the marking criteria before writing, and uses the feedback on each essay to plan the next. Over the term her work improves. What does this show?

_items.text: That working with the whole cycle pays off: reading the design, the criteria and the feedback together kept each piece aimed at the same outcomes.
_items.feedback: Yes. She treated the three parts as one connected cycle, and each piece built on the last.

_items.text: That only the marking criteria matter, and the rest can be ignored.
_items.feedback: She used all three parts, not the criteria alone. Together they kept her work on target.

_items.text: That her tutor marked the later essays more generously.
_items.feedback: The point is not the marking. Her work improved because she worked with the whole cycle.

_items.text: That feedback is useful only at the end of a module.
_items.feedback: She used feedback after each essay, to shape the next. That is the cycle turning.

_feedback.correct: That's right. She read the design, the criteria and the feedback as one connected cycle, so each piece improved on the last.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look at what she did across the whole module, and why her work improved.

displayTitle: You want to use the whole cycle to study {{context}} better this term. Which plan best treats design, marking and feedback as one connected cycle?
body: You want to use the whole cycle to study {{context}} better this term. Which plan best treats design, marking and feedback as one connected cycle?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use the whole cycle to study your subject better this term. Which plan best treats design, marking and feedback as one connected cycle?

_items.text: At the start of each module, work out how it is designed and read its criteria; then use the feedback on each piece to aim the next one better.
_items.feedback: Yes. That works the whole cycle, from design through criteria to feedback, again and again.

_items.text: Focus only on the marking criteria, and ignore how the sessions are designed.
_items.feedback: The design tells you what the sessions are for. Leaving it out breaks the cycle.

_items.text: Wait until the end of the module, then read all the feedback at once.
_items.feedback: Feedback read at the end cannot shape work you have already handed in.

_items.text: Prepare for every session as though it were a lecture, whatever its design.
_items.feedback: That ignores the design. Working with the cycle means engaging with each session on its own terms.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Reading the design and criteria, then acting on feedback each time, keeps the whole cycle turning.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about which plan keeps all three parts of the cycle working together.

displayTitle: What makes a module's design, its marking criteria and its feedback one connected cycle rather than three separate things?
body: What makes a module's design, its marking criteria and its feedback one connected cycle rather than three separate things?

_items.text: They are all aimed at the same intended outcomes, so each part tells you about the others.

_items.text: They are set by three different people who never compare notes.
_items.feedback: They are built around the same outcomes, which is what connects them.

_items.text: They have nothing in common and are best handled separately.
_items.feedback: They share the same outcomes, so each one helps you read the next.

_items.text: Only the marking criteria matter; the other two can be ignored.
_items.feedback: All three parts work together. Leaving one out breaks the cycle.
